subject: surgery
title: Bariatric Surgery, Laparoscopic Sleeve Gastrectomy, and Roux-en-Y Bypass

steps.tx: Metabolic and **bariatric surgery** represents the most effective and durable intervention for achieving substantial long-term weight reduction and resolving obesity-related metabolic comorbidities. Standard indications establish surgical eligibility for patients with a body mass index of forty kilograms per square metre or higher, or a body mass index of thirty-five or higher accompanied by major comorbidities including type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis.
steps.say: Bariatric surgery is indicated for individuals with a BMI of forty or higher, or a BMI of thirty-five or higher with major comorbidities like diabetes or hypertension.

steps.tx: In Asian populations, obesity-related cardiovascular and metabolic risks manifest at lower body mass index thresholds due to higher visceral adiposity. Consequently, revised consensus guidelines reduce the eligibility threshold for Asian patients to a body mass index of **thirty-five kilograms per square metre** without comorbidities, or thirty or higher in the presence of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes or metabolic syndrome.
steps.say: For Asian populations, bariatric criteria are lower: a BMI of thirty-five without comorbidities, or thirty or higher with diabetes, reflecting higher visceral adiposity.

steps.tx: The most commonly performed bariatric procedure globally is the **laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy**. This procedure resects approximately seventy-five to eighty percent of the stomach along the greater curvature, transforming the stomach into a narrow, vertical tubular conduit. By dividing the gastrosplenic and gastrocolic omenta, the surgeon completely mobilizes the greater curvature from two to four centimetres proximal to the pylorus up to the left crus of the diaphragm.
steps.say: Laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy removes seventy-five to eighty percent of the stomach along the greater curvature, leaving a narrow vertical tube calibrated over a bougie.

nodes.label: Laparoscopic Division of Greater Omentum & Short Gastric Vessels
Placement of 36 to 40 French Orogastric Sizing Bougie
Sequential Endoscopic Linear Stapling from Antrum to Angle of His
Extraction of Resected Greater Curvature & Fundus Specimen
Methylene Blue or Air Leak Testing of Long Staple Line

steps.tx: A sizing orogastric bougie measuring thirty-six to forty French is positioned along the lesser curvature to calibrate the diameter of the gastric sleeve, ensuring uniform restriction while preventing luminal stenosis. Resecting the gastric fundus eliminates the primary production site of the orexigenic hunger hormone **ghrelin**. Consequently, patients experience profound post-operative appetite suppression alongside volumetric mechanical restriction, achieving excess weight loss of sixty to seventy percent within twelve months.
steps.say: Sizing over a thirty-six to forty French bougie prevents strictures. Excising the gastric fundus eliminates the hunger hormone ghrelin, suppressing appetite.

right.title: Neuroendocrine Modulation

steps.tx: The most dreaded acute surgical complication following sleeve gastrectomy is a **staple-line leak**, occurring in one to two percent of cases. Over eighty percent of leaks arise at the proximal-most staple line near the gastroesophageal junction, also known as the angle of His. This vulnerable site is prone to localized ischemia from division of the posterior gastric artery, thinner tissue vascularity, and high downstream intra-luminal sleeve pressure.
steps.say: A staple-line leak occurs in up to two percent of sleeve gastrectomies, most commonly at the angle of His near the gastroesophageal junction due to high pressure and ischemia.

nodes.label: Construction of High-Pressure Tubular Gastric Sleeve
Relative Ischemia at Angle of His from Short Gastric Division
Elevated Intraluminal Pressure Against Functional Pylorus
Clinical Unexplained Tachycardia (>120 bpm) Preceding Sepsis

steps.tx: Unexplained persistent **tachycardia exceeding one hundred and twenty beats per minute** is the single earliest and most reliable clinical indicator of an anastomotic or staple-line leak in the bariatric patient. Other signs include tachypnea, fever, left shoulder tip pain, and oliguria. A hemodynamically unstable patient requires immediate emergency laparoscopic exploration, peritoneal lavage, external drain placement, and subsequent endoscopic covered metallic stenting.
steps.say: Persistent tachycardia over one hundred and twenty beats per minute is the earliest sign of a leak. Unstable patients need emergency exploration, drainage, or stenting.

steps.tx: The historic benchmark procedure combining restriction with mild malabsorption is the **Roux-en-Y gastric bypass**. The surgeon creates a tiny fifteen to thirty millilitre gastric pouch, completely transecting it from the excluded gastric remanent. A Roux limb of jejunum measuring seventy-five to one hundred centimetres is anastomosed to the pouch (gastrojejunostomy), while the biliopancreatic limb is connected to the jejunum downstream, bypassing the remaining stomach, duodenum, and proximal jejunum.
steps.say: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass creates a thirty-milliliter gastric pouch connected to a jejunal Roux limb, bypassing the remaining stomach, duodenum, and upper jejunum.

left.title: Sleeve Gastrectomy
points: Technically simpler with zero bowel anastomoses

right.title: Roux-en-Y Bypass
points: Highly effective treatment for severe GERD
Superior long-term remission of type 2 diabetes

steps.tx: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass is the procedure of choice for morbidly obese patients with severe pre-existing gastroesophageal reflux disease or Barrett esophagus, as the low-pressure gastric pouch completely abolishes acid exposure. Specific surgical complications of gastric bypass include **internal herniation** through mesenteric defects (Petersen defect), marginal ulcers at the gastrojejunostomy, and lifelong micronutrient deficiencies requiring daily multivitamin, calcium, iron, and vitamin B12 supplementation.
steps.say: Gastric bypass is ideal for severe acid reflux. Specific complications include internal herniation through Petersen defect and marginal ulcers, requiring lifelong vitamin supplementation.

rows: Bowel herniation through Petersen space defect
Meticulous suture closure of all mesenteric windows
Acid exposure on vulnerable jejunal mucosa
Proton pump inhibitors, strict smoking cessation
Rapid chyme transit into Roux jejunal limb
Bypass of duodenum and proximal jejunum
Lifelong B12, iron, calcium, vitamin D supplements
